La última oportunidad para la paz

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4546 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • PEDRO SÁNCHEZ es presidente del Gobierno de España.
  • En algún momento de la última década, el mundo empezó a aceptar la guerra como algo inevitable.
  • No hay nada más peligroso que normalizar la guerra.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

PEDRO SÁNCHEZ es presidente del Gobierno de España.

Cómo evitar otra guerra mundial.

En algún momento de la última década, el mundo empezó a aceptar la guerra como algo inevitable. Las guerras de agresión, como las de Ucrania, el Líbano o Irán, aumentan y siembran horror, ruina y el temor a una confrontación global. Los gobiernos piensan cada vez más en la guerra como algo para lo que hay que prepararse y presupuestar. El gasto militar no deja de crecer, las carreras tecnológicas y armamentísticas se intensifican, y cada vez más países se plantean si deberían dotarse de un arsenal nuclear disuasorio que garantice su seguridad.

No hay nada más peligroso que normalizar la guerra. Supone regresar a una norma que imperó durante la mayor parte de la historia de la humanidad. La guerra era el eje vertebrador del sistema internacional. Era la vía natural por la que los Estados zanjaban sus disputas o ensanchaban su territorio a costa de vecinos más débiles.

Sources indicate that pero la inmensa devastación que produjeron las dos guerras mundiales en la primera mitad del siglo XX hizo inaceptable ese statu quo. Los países se unieron en un empeño común: que la guerra dejara de ser un instrumento legítimo de la política de Estado y pasara a ser un acto ilegal. Las guerras no terminaron en 1945, pero durante años la comunidad internacional las condenó de forma abrumadora.

Sources indicate that en las últimas décadas, sin embargo, el compromiso de los gobiernos con la causa de la paz se ha debilitado. En 2003, millones de personas salieron a las calles en cientos de ciudades para oponerse a la invasión de Irak liderada por Estados Unidos. Y, aun así, la guerra siguió adelante. Iniciada a partir de premisas falsas y en violación del derecho internacional, arrasó Irak, agravó la inestabilidad regional y avivó el resentimiento y el terrorismo contra los países occidentales. Aquel conflicto marcó, además, un punto de inflexión. Desde entonces, la búsqueda de la paz ha ido retrocediendo en la agenda internacional, arrinconada por la creciente competencia geopolítica y la desatención o la indiferencia hacia los esfuerzos multilaterales que durante décadas pusieron freno a la guerra.

Industry observers note that este camino conduce a una nueva guerra mundial: la catástrofe que el orden del siglo XX se propuso evitar. Ante ese futuro sombrío en el horizonte, los gobiernos deben reaprender el arte de oponerse a la guerra. Todos los países, incluido el mío, España, tienen la responsabilidad de actuar para limitar la capacidad de otros de librar la guerra y para fortalecer las instituciones internacionales que han de ser garantes de la paz.

Sources indicate that el éxito de este proyecto dependerá de un multilateralismo expansivo, al que yo llamo «maxilateralismo»: una cooperación que abarque al mayor número posible de países, en lugar de limitarse a pequeñas coaliciones ad hoc. Su ambición es que la guerra resulte cada vez más inviable, incluso inimaginable. En 2003, manifestantes por toda España coreaban «¡No a la guerra!». En 2026, el mundo no puede volver a ignorarlos.

It has been revealed that los esfuerzos internacionales por desterrar la guerra como instrumento de política nacional se remontan al Pacto Briand-Kellogg de 1928, un tratado firmado en París por 15 países, al que posteriormente se sumaron decenas más. No bastó para impedir la Segunda Guerra Mundial, pero plantó una semilla. Cuando representantes de 50 países se reunieron en San Francisco en 1945 para crear las Naciones Unidas, recuperaron el espíritu y los principios del Pacto y añadieron lo que había faltado: estructura institucional. La Carta de Naciones Unidas prohibió recurrir a la amenaza o al uso de la fuerza contra la integridad territorial o la independencia política de otro Estado. Y, a diferencia de su predecesor de 1928, respaldó esa prohibición con instituciones facultadas para hacerla cumplir.

According to recent reports, en las décadas siguientes, estas instituciones levantaron un orden que castigaba las violaciones al derecho internacional e incentivaba la cooperación y la diplomacia. Al mismo tiempo, el rechazo popular a la guerra y al militarismo de la Guerra Fría cobraba fuerza en todo el mundo. Se hizo visible en la resistencia a la guerra de Vietnam y en los movimientos de masas contra las armas nucleares. El pacifismo alcanzó su punto álgido en los años noventa, cuando una sociedad civil global pujante se movilizó en defensa de causas humanitarias y Naciones Unidas tenía autoridad para abanderar una ambiciosa agenda de paz.

Hoy, sin embargo, hay más conflictos armados que en ningún otro momento desde 1946. Según el Programa de Datos sobre Conflictos de Uppsala, en 2025 hubo 65 conflictos activos con participación estatal, el doble que en 2010. Se calcula que en estos conflictos murieron 250.000 personas: la cifra anual más alta desde el genocidio de Ruanda hace más de 30 años. Cerca de 120 millones de personas en todo el mundo siguen desplazadas por la guerra.

Y lo más inquietante: las guerras de agresión, que violan la Carta de Naciones Unidas, están de vuelta. Rusia invadió Ucrania. Estados Unidos e Israel atacaron Irán. Y mientras los combates se prolongan año tras año en lugares como el Líbano, Sudán o Yemen, resulta evidente que la guerra está siendo aceptada de nuevo como algo normal.

Industry observers note that nada indica que esta tendencia vaya a frenarse. Los presupuestos militares se han disparado hasta niveles no vistos en generaciones, en detrimento del gasto social y de desarrollo. Solo en la última década, el gasto mundial en defensa ha aumentado más de un 40 %, y muchos países han duplicado sus presupuestos militares. Los casi 3 billones de dólares que el mundo destina cada año a defensa se acercan al producto interior bruto de todo el continente africano. Incluso países con una larga tradición de contención militar, como Alemania, Dinamarca, Japón y Noruega, se están rearmando a toda velocidad, y algunos están recuperando el servicio militar.

Aún más estremecedor es el regreso de la amenaza de guerra nuclear. Los nueve Estados con armas nucleares están modernizando sus arsenales y aumentando su capacidad destructiva. Se calcula que el arsenal de China ha pasado de entre unas 200-300 cabezas nucleares a finales de la década de 2010 a 620 este año. Corea del Norte también ha ampliado el suyo, de entre 10-20 cabezas estimadas en 2018 a unas 60 este año, y ha desarrollado plataformas de lanzamiento cada vez más sofisticadas. En marzo, Francia anunció el primer aumento de su número de cabezas nucleares desde 1992. Estados Unidos y Rusia, las dos mayores potencias nucleares del mundo, no han sido capaces de preservar el último tratado que ponía límites a sus arsenales estratégicos. Y cada vez más potencias no nucleares han empezado a plantearse adquirir armas nucleares propias.

Al mismo tiempo, la inteligencia artificial (IA) está dotando a la guerra de armas cada vez más peligrosas. La supervisión humana se reduce progresivamente a medida que la IA permite automatizar ciberataques contra redes eléctricas, hospitales y sistemas financieros. Hay sistemas de IA que ya han logrado infiltrarse en organismos públicos y han hecho posible la producción masiva de deepfakes y de campañas de desinformación.

La integración de la IA en las tecnologías nucleares es una amenaza existencial: al acelerar la toma de decisiones, comprime el tiempo disponible para el juicio humano. Del mismo modo, el uso de la IA en biotecnología podría rebajar drásticamente las barreras a la experimentación nociva y al desarrollo de armas biológicas. En ambos terrenos, esta tecnología está elevando a niveles sin precedentes el riesgo de errores de cálculo, de escaladas involuntarias y de destrucción masiva.

En conjunto, estas dinámicas multiplican las probabilidades de que cualquier crisis desemboque rápidamente en la aniquilación del planeta. Por desgracia, los países están fabricando los instrumentos de la catástrofe a la velocidad vertiginosa de la innovación, mientras que los instrumentos de control avanzan al ritmo, mucho más lento, de la diplomacia.

It has been revealed that los cambios políticos están alejando al mundo de la paz. Lo empujan hacia la militarización y la confrontación. Un mundo multipolar no es, por definición, más peligroso. Pero la erosión de las normas y de las instituciones que deberían encauzar las tensiones entre los distintos polos está provocando que el mundo se vuelva especialmente volátil. La competencia entre grandes potencias se intensifica: las ansias de hegemonía alientan políticas exteriores agresivas y los Estados revisionistas desafían las normas y las fronteras establecidas. El nacionalismo beligerante crece. Los movimientos de extrema derecha promueven una visión del mundo en la que las relaciones internacionales son un juego de suma cero y los países deben competir en lugar de cooperar. Incluso dirigentes de centro están adoptando la retórica de la guerra. Aunque no pretendan iniciar una, sus palabras abonan una mentalidad militarista peligrosa.

En este clima de rivalidad, las guerras de agresión se envuelven en discursos de necesidad, liberación, legítima defensa o justicia histórica. Los agresores presentan sus operaciones como inevitables, después de haber demonizado a sus adversarios para justificar un ataque preventivo. Venden cada guerra como la respuesta a la inseguridad: la guerra que acabará con todas las guerras.

In a recent development, pero estas guerras no harán del mundo un lugar más seguro. Cada vez que un Estado desata una guerra de agresión, erosiona las normas que protegen a todos los países frente al uso arbitrario de la fuerza, incluido el propio Estado agresor.

According to recent reports, las guerras tienen un coste inmenso. Destrozan sociedades y truncan vidas. En 2025, según los registros de Naciones Unidas, al menos un civil murió en conflicto armado cada 14 minutos, y más de cinco millones de personas se vieron obligadas a huir de sus países. El coste económico también es altísimo. La guerra que enfrenta a Estados Unidos e Israel con Irán ha alterado gravemente el comercio marítimo y el tráfico aéreo y ha disparado los precios de la energía, los fertilizantes y otras materias primas. Millones de personas en todo el mundo están sufriendo las consecuencias.

La guerra genera, además, nuevos peligros. Una vez que empiezan los combates, su rumbo es imprevisible. Los conflictos tienden a arrastrar a nuevos actores y a desbordarse hacia los países vecinos. La guerra de Irán vuelve a ser un ejemplo claro. Desde febrero de 2026, Irán ha atacado objetivos en varios países del Golfo y de su entorno, acciones que España ha condenado sin excepción. Los ataques contra buques civiles y mercantes amenazan la estabilidad del conjunto de la región. Y la guerra ha reavivado los conflictos de Irak, el Líbano y Yemen.

Por último, las guerras rara vez traen una paz duradera. Al contrario: ahondan los agravios y enquistan las divisiones que alimentan la violencia del mañana. La guerra de Rusia en Ucrania, por ejemplo, ha dinamitado la confianza en Moscú. El genocidio en Gaza ha exacerbado la indignación contra Israel, y eso podría desembocar en nuevas oleadas de terrorismo. Y la guerra contra Irán ha desestabilizado aún más la región y ha lastrado la cooperación entre sus países.

El mundo tiene la responsabilidad de resistirse a la normalización de la guerra. Callar es un acto de cobardía y de complicidad. La sociedad española está dejando clara su posición: tres de cada cuatro españoles señalan la guerra como su mayor temor. Y un número aún mayor cree que se cierne otra guerra mundial.

Sources indicate that pero no basta con condenar la guerra en abstracto. La ambición de acabar con ella debe ir acompañada de acciones concretas que hagan cada vez más difícil que los países inicien, sostengan y justifiquen un conflicto armado.

Recent findings suggest that españa ha procurado actuar en esa dirección. Ha defendido las normas internacionales que marcan la diferencia entre un orden basado en reglas y otro gobernado por la fuerza. Y ha denunciado siempre los ataques armados que violan la Carta de Naciones Unidas.

Recent findings suggest that desde el primer día de la guerra en Gaza, España ha reclamado un alto el fuego inmediato y permanente, la liberación de todos los rehenes y la entrada sin restricciones de la ayuda humanitaria. En mayo de 2024, España reconoció el Estado de Palestina con la esperanza de que este paso contribuyera a avanzar hacia una solución negociada y duradera del conflicto. Y ha apoyado activamente los esfuerzos de la Corte Internacional de Justicia y de la Corte Penal Internacional para que los dirigentes israelíes rindan cuentas por sus violaciones del derecho internacional humanitario. Israel tenía derecho a la legítima defensa tras los atentados terroristas del 7 de octubre. Pero ese derecho no justifica el genocidio en Gaza ni la expansión de la ocupación ilegal de Cisjordania.

Disuadir la guerra exige también elevar el coste de la agresión. El resto del mundo debe asegurarse de que quien elija hacer la guerra no pueda hacerlo sin pagar un precio. A lo largo de la invasión rusa de Ucrania, por ejemplo, la Unión Europea ha aprobado sucesivas rondas de sanciones contra Rusia que España ha respaldado sin titubeos. España también ha prestado a Ucrania ayuda financiera, humanitaria y militar para que pueda defender su territorio y negarle a Rusia el botín de guerra.

Sources indicate that los países deben negarse a ayudar a las partes a extender los conflictos en curso. España, por ejemplo, mantiene un embargo de armas a Israel desde 2023. Este año, además, negó a Estados Unidos el uso de su territorio y de sus instalaciones para la guerra contra Irán. La decisión de España no fue un acto de hostilidad hacia un aliado. Tampoco fue una expresión de neutralidad ni de simpatía hacia el régimen iraní. Fue el fruto de una valoración estratégica: implicarse habría favorecido la escalada del conflicto y agravado la inseguridad regional y mundial. Para ser fiel a su compromiso con la paz, España tenía que estar dispuesta a decir no, aunque eso tuviera un coste político. Si más países hubieran actuado igual, las guerras de Gaza y de Irán habrían sido mucho más difíciles y costosas de librar.

Sources indicate that invertir en prosperidad es igualmente esencial. La seguridad crece cuando las sociedades son resilientes, las desigualdades se reducen y la ciudadanía puede confiar en las instituciones públicas. La decisión de España, el año pasado, de no asumir el objetivo de gasto en defensa del 5 % del PIB propuesto por la OTAN refleja esta visión. No nace de una falta de compromiso con la defensa europea. De hecho, mi Gobierno ha sido uno de los principales impulsores de la autonomía estratégica de la Unión Europea, triplicando el gasto neto en defensa en los ocho años que llevo en el cargo. Pero la disuasión militar y el bienestar social deben reforzarse mutuamente. Al mantener un gasto en defensa proporcionado, España ha conservado el margen fiscal necesario para invertir 145.000 millones de euros adicionales en protección social, vivienda, sanidad y educación, y más de 30.000 millones en la transición ecológica. Son políticas que cohesionan la sociedad y, por tanto, la hacen más segura.

Los esfuerzos de un solo país tienen, sin embargo, un alcance limitado. Cortarle el oxígeno a la guerra exige la implicación de todos: un esfuerzo colectivo basado en un multilateralismo genuino. Esta es la única estrategia que ha funcionado en el pasado. El sistema multilateral construido tras la Segunda Guerra Mundial abarcaba todo el planeta y contribuyó a preservar la paz entre las grandes potencias y a evitar una tercera guerra mundial.

In a recent development, reforzarlo no será tarea fácil. La pugna geopolítica y una desconfianza generalizada han debilitado a Naciones Unidas, los organismos financieros internacionales, las organizaciones regionales y otras instituciones multilaterales. Muchos países las perciben como ineficaces y atrapadas en una crisis perpetua, de modo que están recurriendo a marcos alternativos para intentar poner fin a las guerras.

According to recent reports, algunos han optado por enfoques unilaterales, persiguiendo acuerdos transaccionales que acaban beneficiando a élites económicas y políticas y dejan al margen a las poblaciones afectadas por el conflicto. Los altos el fuego o los acuerdos de paz que logran pueden ser preferibles a la continuación de la guerra, pero cualquier paz impuesta por la ley del más fuerte, y no por el derecho, se asienta sobre cimientos frágiles.

Otros países, frustrados con el multilateralismo, han intentado formar «coaliciones de voluntarios» u otros grupos «minilaterales» para garantizar su seguridad o alcanzar acuerdos ad hoc en materia de comercio o tecnología. Este enfoque puede ser una solución temporal a la parálisis de las instituciones tradicionales, pero su carácter excluyente fragmenta aún más un orden internacional ya dividido. Lo que necesitamos no es minilateralismo, sino maxilateralismo. La cooperación internacional alcanza su verdadera fuerza cuando es—o aspira a ser—universal. Dejar a una parte del mundo fuera de estos esfuerzos es, además, incubar la confrontación de mañana.

El sistema internacional del siglo XX no era perfecto. Sus normas se han aplicado de manera desigual, sus principios se han defendido de forma inconsistente y sus procedimientos han sido desesperantemente lentos. Pero es innegable que, sin él, el mundo sería un polvorín aún mayor. Basta un ejemplo: fue una red de tratados internacionales—entre ellos, el Tratado sobre la No Proliferación de las Armas Nucleares, el Tratado sobre Fuerzas Nucleares de Alcance Intermedio y el Tratado de Prohibición Parcial de los Ensayos Nucleares—la que puso fin a una carrera armamentística desbocada y extraordinariamente costosa que estaba llevando al mundo al borde de una guerra nuclear.

Toda esta arquitectura institucional se está resquebrajando. Y sin ella, aspirar a preservar la paz es una quimera.

Recent findings suggest that fortalecer las instituciones multilaterales debe ser el eje central de una campaña global para relegar la guerra a los libros de historia. Para ello será necesario acometer reformas de calado que les devuelvan la legitimidad y refuercen su capacidad de actuación, dando prioridad a las medidas que más contribuyan a la paz y la seguridad.

Industry observers note that la primera pasa por aumentar la representación en las Naciones Unidas y las instituciones de Bretton Woods. Actualizar la estructura del Consejo de Seguridad de Naciones Unidas es especialmente importante, dada su responsabilidad principal de mantener la paz internacional. Un Consejo de Seguridad con asientos permanentes y derecho de veto para las cinco potencias vencedoras de la Segunda Guerra Mundial, que en conjunto suman apenas una cuarta parte de la población mundial, no refleja el mundo de hoy. Debe ampliarse el número de miembros electos del Consejo y alargar su mandato más allá de los dos años actuales. Los nuevos asientos deben otorgarse principalmente a países de regiones infrarrepresentadas, en particular África y América Latina. Organizaciones regionales como la Unión Europea y la Unión Africana también deberían estar representadas en el Consejo, posiblemente ocupando puestos que hoy corresponden a Estados. Un Consejo de Seguridad más representativo no solo sería más justo, sino también más eficaz. Los países defienden y hacen cumplir con más empeño las normas internacionales cuando se sienten autores de ellas.

Industry observers note that también hay que restringir estrictamente el poder de veto de los miembros permanentes, en especial cuando el Consejo de Seguridad delibere sobre casos de atrocidades masivas, genocidio, crímenes de lesa humanidad y crímenes de guerra. En última instancia, el veto debe abolirse por completo. Solo entonces podrá el Consejo responder a todos los actos de agresión sin quedar secuestrado por las objeciones de un solo Estado.

Recent findings suggest that un espíritu similar debería orientar la transformación estructural de las instituciones financieras internacionales, en particular el Fondo Monetario Internacional y el Banco Mundial. La distribución del poder de voto en ambas sigue reflejando los equilibrios económicos del siglo XX y, por convención, un europeo está siempre al frente del FMI y un estadounidense, del Banco Mundial. Esto debe terminar. Las economías emergentes necesitan una representación más adecuada, y los puestos de liderazgo deben estar abiertos a todos los candidatos, sea cual sea su nacionalidad. También deberán evolucionar las responsabilidades que asumen en instituciones como la Organización Mundial del Comercio los países antes considerados «en desarrollo», a medida que crecen y se incorporan al grupo de las economías más ricas. Una gobernanza económica más justa aliviaría la desigualdad y el resentimiento que con tanta frecuencia atizan la inestabilidad y los conflictos.

In a recent development, otra reforma esencial consiste en revitalizar el marco internacional que contiene el riesgo de escalada nuclear. Parte de ese trabajo depende de las potencias nucleares. Corresponde a Estados Unidos y a Rusia negociar un tratado que suceda al acuerdo bilateral Nuevo START y que preserve topes verificables al despliegue de armas nucleares. Y, esta vez, China debería participar en las conversaciones.

Pero el esfuerzo más amplio exige el compromiso de todos los países. Entre sus prioridades deben figurar la ratificación del Tratado de Prohibición Completa de los Ensayos Nucleares, para impedir que se reanuden las pruebas nucleares, y el avance de las negociaciones sobre un Tratado de Prohibición de la Producción de Material Fisionable, que prohibiría la producción de uranio altamente enriquecido y plutonio para armas nucleares. Todos deben también trabajar conjuntamente para regular el uso de la IA en el ámbito militar, especialmente en lo que respecta a las armas nucleares, a fin de preservar el control humano sobre las decisiones de lanzamiento y minimizar el riesgo de errores fatales. Los países no nucleares deben comprometerse a no adquirir armas nucleares y deben emplear todos los medios a su alcance para instar a las potencias nucleares a reducir sus arsenales, reforzar los mecanismos de verificación y reconstruir las salvaguardas diplomáticas que durante décadas han ayudado a evitar una catástrofe nuclear.

La tecnología puede contribuir en parte a esta tarea. Los avances en imágenes por satélite, sensores remotos y análisis de datos pueden aumentar la transparencia y la supervisión del cumplimiento de los acuerdos de control de armamentos. Pero también hay que hacer mucho más para evitar situaciones que puedan precipitar una guerra. Si los Estados con armas nucleares acuerdan reducir su disponibilidad operacional y reforzar la comunicación en momentos de tensión, los gobiernos contarán con más tiempo y más medios para desactivar las crisis. Cada país debe proteger sus sistemas de mando y control frente a los ciberataques y la manipulación informativa impulsada por la IA, de modo que una falsa alarma o un error de cálculo no desencadenen jamás una guerra nuclear.

Por último, es prioritario trabajar para garantizar que el sistema de justicia internacional pueda hacer cumplir las decisiones de los tribunales. Desmantelar la Corte Penal Internacional, como pretenden algunos países, solo aseguraría la impunidad de los crímenes más atroces. La CPI no solo debe investigar y juzgar los casos de genocidio, agresión, crímenes de guerra y crímenes de lesa humanidad, sino también contar con la autoridad necesaria para llevar ante la justicia a los responsables de esos crímenes. Cuando un Estado pasa a ser parte del Estatuto de Roma, el tratado que creó la CPI, acepta someterse a la jurisdicción de la Corte. Sin embargo, si ese Estado se niega a cooperar o a entregar a un sospechoso, no existe una sanción efectiva, sino apenas una llamada de atención. Esto debe cambiar. Los Estados que den cobijo a personas imputadas por la CPI deben afrontar consecuencias legales, diplomáticas y financieras. Iniciar y librar una guerra debe tener un coste real.

La reforma de las instituciones internacionales lleva años estancada, pero la próxima elección para la Secretaría General de Naciones Unidas ofrece una ocasión excepcional para darle un nuevo impulso. Que Naciones Unidas nombrara a su primera secretaria general sería un poderoso símbolo de renovación, inclusión y adaptación institucional. La organización no puede afirmar verdaderamente que habla en nombre de toda la humanidad mientras no la haya dirigido una mujer. Alcanzar este hito podría despertar una nueva ambición y reforzar la confianza en la capacidad de las instituciones internacionales para reformarse y para que recuperen su papel a la hora de poner freno a la guerra.

Frenar la deriva del mundo hacia la guerra exigirá el compromiso más amplio posible. Ningún país, grande o pequeño, puede mirar hacia otro lado ni sumarse a las acciones que aviven la escalada. Todos debemos defender las normas internacionales que hoy ponen coto a la guerra y reformar y dotar de poder a las instituciones que mañana la harán imposible.

En última instancia, lo que hará inimaginable la guerra es una agenda de paz positiva que aborde las causas profundas de la inseguridad. Cada paso hacia la erradicación de la pobreza, la ampliación del acceso a una educación de calidad, el avance de la igualdad de género, el fortalecimiento de las instituciones democráticas y el aumento de la resiliencia ante los desastres naturales atenúa también las condiciones que engendran la violencia.

Las instituciones financieras internacionales deben ser capaces de proporcionar financiación con rapidez, a gran escala y a un coste razonable, para que ningún país en desarrollo se vea obligado a elegir entre atender su deuda e invertir en su población. Los bancos multilaterales de desarrollo deben poder movilizar fondos para las transiciones ecológica y digital, de modo que las migraciones climáticas y la disputa por los recursos no se conviertan en detonantes de conflictos entre Estados. Y el Acuerdo sobre Pandemias de la Organización Mundial de la Salud debe ultimarse y entrar en vigor para garantizar que todos los países puedan acceder a vacunas y tratamientos cuando llegue la próxima emergencia sanitaria mundial.

Por eso España ha procurado situar el desarrollo en el centro de su política exterior. El Gobierno español ha sido un firme defensor de los Objetivos de Desarrollo Sostenible de la ONU para 2030 y, el año pasado, la ciudad de Sevilla acogió la Cuarta Conferencia Internacional sobre la Financiación para el Desarrollo, donde la comunidad internacional se comprometió a aligerar la carga de la deuda de los países vulnerables y a desbloquear inversiones para el desarrollo sostenible. España también ha promovido iniciativas como el Centro Global para Canjes de Deuda por Desarrollo, lanzado junto con el Banco Mundial; la Alianza multilateral por las Cláusulas de Suspensión de Deuda, que permite a los países vulnerables suspender el pago de su deuda tras una catástrofe; y un mecanismo propio para ofrecer hasta 60 millones de euros anuales en alivio de deuda a países en desarrollo. Además, España ha respaldado, junto con instituciones multilaterales y organizaciones internacionales, iniciativas de financiación climática, salud global, igualdad de género, seguridad alimentaria y protección social. Estas políticas de desarrollo son también políticas de construcción de paz.

Un proyecto ambicioso de movilización global en favor del derecho internacional y de un multilateralismo genuino puede parecer poco realista. Pero ya hemos visto lo que ocurre cuando la normalización de la guerra arrastra a la humanidad al infierno. Los hombres y las mujeres que se levantaron de entre las ruinas de la Segunda Guerra Mundial, el capítulo más oscuro de nuestra historia, encontraron la manera de construir un orden mundial multilateral. La pregunta a la que se enfrenta nuestra generación es si seremos capaces de preservar el imperio de la ley o permitiremos el regreso de la ley de la jungla. Si construiremos el mundo del mañana con visión de futuro y cooperación, o a través del caos y del dolor de otra guerra mundial. Debemos elegir bien mientras la decisión siga estando en nuestras manos.

Speaker Mike Johnson calls upon House Republicans to show up for work

Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram breaks down the progressive pushback House Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries faces after winning the Democratic nomination. Pergram also discusses how Democratic demands for Medicare-for-all and aggressive congressional investigations could test party unity.

House Speaker Mike Johnson issued a message Friday calling on his colleagues to show up for work so Republicans can advance their priorities before Democrats take over the chamber next year.

It has been revealed that "This week we had to postpone the rule scheduled for the Floor because we didn't have enough Members in town. To state the obvious, barring any serious medical problem, we need every Republican to be here to faithfully complete our full two-year term," Johnson wrote.

"Over the next 44 days, we need every House Republican to remain fully engaged so we can get even more of our important priorities signed into law.".

MIKE JOHNSON NOT RUNNING TO LEAD HOUSE GOP AFTER HISTORIC MIDTERM LOSSES.

U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson speaks before presenting Gamal El Sadat with the Congressional Gold Medal, posthumously honoring his father, former Egyptian President Anwar Sadat, at Statuary Hall in the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., Nov. 18, 2026. (Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images).

While Democrats routed Republicans during the 2026 midterms and will consequently have majorities in both chambers of Congress next year, Republicans still control the House and Senate majorities.

"The Twentieth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution specifies that our clock doesn't run out until noon on January 3rd. LET'S SCORE EVERY POINT WE CAN AND LEAVE IT ALL ON THE FIELD!" Johnson urged in the letter.

It has been revealed that "You don’t deserve a paycheck when you don’t show up for work. And the American people aren’t happy to hear their elected officials want to stay home. Our work is far from over," Norman asserted.

Shenzhen Was No Yalta Conference

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s China Brief.

The highlights this week: The presidents of China, Russia, and the United States hold a historic trilateral summit in Shenzhen, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi receives a cold welcome in China, and fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s scandal continues.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s China Brief.

The highlights this week: The presidents of China, Russia, and the United States hold a historic trilateral summit in Shenzhen, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi receives a cold welcome in China, and fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s scandal continues.

The first-ever trilateral meeting among the leaders of China, Russia, and the United States—held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) gathering this week in Shenzhen, China—was, as expected, little more than a photo opportunity.

Still, all three will be pleased with the pictures. U.S. President Donald Trump, smarting from his party’s overwhelming defeat in the midterm elections, gets to play statesman. Russian President Vladimir Putin gets to play peacemaker. And Chinese President Xi Jinping gets to play the man in charge—though nowadays that may be more accurate than not.

The official joint statement from the summit, issued by Chinese state news agency Xinhua, echoed themes that Xi has promoted throughout Trump’s second term: strategic stability, opposition to Cold War thinking and economic decoupling, and respect for the outcomes of World War II.

Sources indicate that china and Russia routinely trot out that final point to justify their territorial claims today. The irony is rich for China, which was represented during the war by leaders of the Republic of China government, who later fled to Taiwan. (In Eastern Europe, meanwhile, the victorious power was the Soviet Union, not Russia.).

Before the meeting, there was talk that the Shenzhen trilateral might amount to a upcoming Yalta Conference—the 1945 summit at which the three main victors of World War II divided up Europe.

This speculation drew on the long-simmering idea that the world might once again be carved into spheres of influence. But the idea that a upcoming Yalta is possible at all is fundamentally misguided. Two of the three great powers today are bogged down in economically devastating wars of choice against smaller countries.

It has been revealed that crucially, it is clear that the world is not theirs to divide. Trump cannot force Ukraine to surrender or hand Taiwan to Beijing. Putin cannot restore Soviet grandeur by force. And China, for all its bluster, has yet to bring Taiwan to heel.

According to recent reports, the Yalta fantasy also ignores how much weaker today’s great powers are than their 1945 counterparts. At the time, the Soviet military was the largest in the world, the U.S. economy was bigger than those of the rest of the developed world combined, and the diminished United Kingdom still ruled an empire that encompassed one-quarter of the global population.

Nor did the Yalta bargain of a world divided among superpowers hold. Rather than securing a lasting peace, it laid the groundwork for the Cold War and spawned bloodshed from Korea to Hungary within a few years. A grand bargain among China, Russia, and the United States today is even less likely to work.

For all the talk of a new world order, the summit produced little of substance. The three powers nominally agreed to engage in dialogue on reducing nuclear risks, but with no advance diplomatic work and significant differences among their arsenals, not much will come of it.

Sources indicate that the joint statement did have one effect, though. The leaders’ condemnation of the International Criminal Court handed China and Russia ideological ammunition, reinforcing the autocratic disdain for international institutions and human rights that all countries are meant to uphold.

But Beijing should not mistake the summit for a license to keep the terms of U.S.-China talks strictly about power. With Democrats set to take control of key China-related committees in the U.S. Congress in January, issues involving democracy and political dissidents will take on renewed importance, no matter what Trump or Xi would prefer.

Takaichi receives cold welcome. Hosting the APEC gathering gave China another opportunity to signal its displeasure with Japan. The bilateral relationship is still at a nadir, more than a year after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said a Chinese invasion of Taiwan could justify Japanese intervention.

Sources indicate that as other leaders were greeted with fanfare, Takaichi was received at Shenzhen’s airport by a relatively low-ranking diplomat. I suspect there was also implicit misogyny at play: Chinese state media has denigrated Takaichi in sexist terms, as it did with former Taiwanese President Tsai Ing-wen.

Though Takaichi was largely sidelined at the APEC meeting, she did what she could to meet bilaterally with other leaders instead.

Sources indicate that A magisterial China resource. Last month, scholar Endymion Wilkinson published the eighth edition of Chinese History: A Latest Manual, one of the most notable books in the field of China studies. First published in 1973 as a relatively slim research guide of around 70,000 words, it now approaches 2 million and covers everything from Chinese cuisine to politics.

Industry observers note that wilkinson is now 85, but each latest edition still contains substantial revisions and additions. The latest includes personal recollections from his stints in China: first as an English teacher at Peking University on the eve of the Cultural Revolution and later as the European Union’s ambassador from 1994 to 2001.

A remarkable work of erudition and dedication, the book remains a starting point for virtually any research into China.

Nvidia scandal updates. The fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s marital infidelities continues to widen, with the manufacturer facing legal scrutiny and a wider crackdown on U.S. chip exports. Huang had an affair with alleged Chinese asset Alice Huang; he resigned from his role last week and is set to testify before the U.S. Congress early next month.

In a recent development, reporting suggests that Nvidia’s involvement in networks designed to evade U.S. export controls lies somewhere between active complicity and willful blindness. Alice Huang’s husband, who reportedly knew about the affair, also played a major part in building state-backed data centers designed to give China access to more computing power.

Alice Huang is now back in Beijing, beyond the reach of potential criminal charges in Singapore.

It has been revealed that U.S. cybersecurity risks? As many tech services seemed to break in the last week, many people asked whether the outages were an ordinary screwup or a cyberattack. The consensus so far is that the problems were unrelated, caused by companies rushing to upgrade systems before the holidays.

But it’s worth remembering that China achieved deep penetration of U.S. infrastructure with Volt Typhoon, a state-sponsored hacking group, which was publicly exposed in 2024. The Trump administration dismantled the expert groups investigating Volt Typhoon early last year, and China could likely still shut down large parts of U.S. life if it chose to do so.

#76986. China Doesn’t Want a Nuclear Arms Race

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2786 w)

China Doesn’t Want a Nuclear Arms Race

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2786 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GOLDSTEIN is Director of the Asia Program at Defense Priorities and Director of the China Initiative at Brown University’s Watson School of International and Public Affairs.
  • NINA TANNENWALD is Associate Teaching Professor of Political Science at Brown University.
  • Industry observers note that today, pessimism—almost fatalism—reigns in Washington about the United States’ ability to avoid a costly and dangerous arms race with China.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LYLE J. GOLDSTEIN is Director of the Asia Program at Defense Priorities and Director of the China Initiative at Brown University’s Watson School of International and Public Affairs.

NINA TANNENWALD is Associate Teaching Professor of Political Science at Brown University.

How America Can Avert an Unnecessary Rivalry.

Sources indicate that lyle J. Goldstein and Nina Tannenwald.

Industry observers note that today, pessimism—almost fatalism—reigns in Washington about the United States’ ability to avoid a costly and dangerous arms race with China. Policymakers point to China’s increasingly aggressive policies toward Taiwan, its massive military buildup, and its resistance to engaging in some arms control measures as evidence that Beijing has accepted the inevitability of such a race or is even pursuing one. Worried by intellectual frameworks that emphasize the likelihood of war between rival great powers, many U.S. leaders and analysts see little choice but for the United States to arm itself, too. But this thinking risks becoming a self-fulling prophecy. The major danger is that an unrestrained arms race increases the likelihood of war over Taiwan or even of a catastrophic nuclear exchange.

Sources indicate that but the pessimism about averting an arms race is misplaced. A nuclear arms race, in particular, is not a foregone conclusion—and the United States has real opportunities to curb one. Avoiding a nuclear arms race will require a broader approach than the two-pronged one Washington has recently favored: building up U.S. nuclear deterrence and seeking to force concessions from Beijing by imposing restrictions on trade and technology transfers. American leaders should instead look beyond traditional deterrence, which falls short because its threat-based approach tends to provoke competition over arms, and strive to establish a more fundamental strategic stability through a process of reciprocal de-escalation and compromise. China is likely to be amenable to reciprocal de-escalation: it has a long tradition of moderation in nuclear matters and, ultimately, Chinese leaders do not want a war over Taiwan.

There are recent signs that even U.S. President Donald Trump, who has often boasted about his distaste for compromise, sees the value of engagement. After two U.S.-Chinese bilateral summits this year, in October he suggested that his November trilateral meeting in Shenzhen with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin should focus on “denuclearization.” But Washington will have to become much more consistent in its rejection of an arms race, including by modifying its support for Taiwan and incorporating China into global arms control leadership. A nuclear arms race with China becomes inevitable only if Washington continues to believe it is.

Industry observers note that china is undoubtedly pursuing a military buildup, including investments in nuclear weapons. Between 2020 and 2025, China doubled the number of its nuclear warheads, from 300 to 600—a startling increase, although its arsenal remains small compared with the United States’ approximately 3,700 warheads. In 2021, researchers at the Federation of American Scientists announced that China was constructing 350 latest nuclear missile silos in three vast sites in Xinjiang and Gansu provinces. Beijing is also pursuing substantial qualitative upgrades to its nuclear weapons, a push it showcased at an October 2025 military parade that unveiled a new sea-rolled out ballistic missile, two new kinds of intercontinental ballistic missiles, a new air-launched hypersonic missile, and a new long-range hypersonic cruise missile.

Sources indicate that then, this July, the Chinese navy tested a submarine-debuted long-range ballistic missile that could carry nuclear weapons. This significant latest capability will allow China to launch long-range nuclear strikes that can reach the United States from protected waters near its own coastline rather than having to sail out into the Pacific. A recent editorial in a leading Chinese foreign affairs newspaper took the candid yet disturbing step of explicitly linking China’s rapid nuclear buildup to its desire to exert sovereignty over Taiwan. “The great cause of national reunification,” it asserted, “must rest on a solid, realistic foundation. That foundation is, first and foremost, hard power.” Although such overt nuclear saber rattling remains rare, the link between Beijing’s nuclear forces and the Taiwan matter stretches back over three decades and is also supported by the scholar Tong Zhao’s detailed analysis of China’s nuclear buildup in Foreign Affairs in May.

As China builds up its military, the perception that it is on a collision course with the United States over Taiwan—one that inevitably includes the risk of nuclear escalation—has become widespread in Washington. Taiwan, of course, appears to be an obvious flash point. The United States has long committed itself informally to defending the island while China seeks to unify with it, by force if necessary. In October, Army General Ronald Clark, the head of the U.S. Pacific Command, affirmed that his forces are actively readying for a Chinese invasion of Taiwan that could come as early as 2027.

It has been revealed that the Biden administration and both Trump administrations made some attempts to engage China over arms control and nuclear risk reduction. Trump proposed trilateral arms control talks that would include Russia, whereas the Biden administration pursued bilateral talks with China on strategic stability and nuclear risk reduction. But both presidents gave up after China consistently rejected engaging in sustained talks on nuclear matters. Beijing’s stance is that it has a small nuclear arsenal compared with the United States and Russia and that it is important to first establish trust and mutual reassurance about core interests.

Beyond China’s resistance to arms control, theories about power that are trendy in Washington reinforce the collision course mentality. Numerous realist scholars argue that a U.S.-Chinese rivalry and even a great-power war may be structurally difficult to avoid. The political scientist Graham Allison captured this pessimism in his influential 2017 book, Destined for War, which argued that a so-called Thucydides trap—when a rapidly rising power challenges the position of the dominant power, yielding war—would doom the United States and China to conflict.

China hawks, such as Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby, increasingly advocate an aggressive focus on “preparing for World War III” with China as a way to avoid it. In a July Upcoming York Times interview, Colby argued that the United States must “deny” China “the ability to seize and hold the key territory” of Taiwan, by enhancing U.S. deterrence with a massive military buildup. The next month, speaking at a military conference, Colby specified that such a buildup ought to put a greater emphasis on tactical nuclear weapons and the ability to fight a so-called limited nuclear war. The enemy, Colby said, has “got to believe there’s some sense in which we would use” nuclear weapons. Toward this end, the United States is building a new intercontinental ballistic missile, a new air-introduced cruise missile, and new nuclear-armed submarines and bombers, and accelerating the ambitious Golden Dome homeland missile defense project. Unlike earlier U.S. missile defenses, which were designed to intercept limited strikes by so called rogue states such as Iran and North Korea, the Golden Dome is intended to defend against massive Chinese or Russian attacks. But the prospect of losing its ability to retaliate against a U.S. first strike only gives Beijing more incentive to expand its nuclear arsenal.

Such a nuclear-heavy approach only prevents a war with China if nuclear deterrence succeeds. That puts a lot of eggs in the deterrence basket. And recent wars suggest that nuclear deterrence is becoming less effective. Russia’s nuclear threats have not coerced Ukraine into halting its strikes deep into Russian territory. Iran has proved willing to launch strikes against nuclear-armed Israel as well as U.S. bases and allies in the Middle East. What is most ominous, in May 2025, India and Pakistan crossed previous redlines and attacked each other’s homelands, something that mutual nuclear deterrence was supposed to prevent. Even if neither the United States nor China want nuclear war, a China determined to unify with Taiwan may not be intimidated by U.S. nuclear threats.

A recent study by Brown University’s Costs of War program found that the United States has already spent more than $3.4 trillion on its militarized rivalry with China over the last decade. Sustaining or ramping up this spending—which encompasses fresh warships, aircraft, long-range missiles, drones, base upgrades, forward deployments, large military exercises, research and development, and new nuclear weapons—is infeasible in an era of ballooning national debt and expanding domestic needs.

Industry observers note that one of the tragedies of an arms race is that neither party may actually want to pursue one. Despite its current arms buildup, Beijing has a long record of moderation in military and nuclear matters. For many decades, it has maintained a minimal nuclear deterrent and a no-first-use policy, and it did not use major military force to achieve strategic goals. Although it has long had access to the relevant technologies, China appears not to have produced or deployed tactical nuclear weapons. Chinese diplomats played a substantial role in coaxing Iran to accept the Obama administration’s 2015 nuclear deal and supported the UN’s relatively stringent sanctions on North Korea. And in the fall of 2022, according to then Secretary of State Antony Blinken and reporting by the Financial Times, China likely intervened diplomatically with the Kremlin to help stop Russia from using nuclear weapons in Ukraine. More broadly, China has embraced international law when it comes to war, playing a constructive role, for example, in removing chemical weapons from Syria in 2013.

Beijing’s inclination toward restraint has not disappeared completely, even as it upgrades its military. In November 2023, U.S. President Joe Biden and Xi agreed to renew lines of communication between their countries’ militaries that had been severed after U.S. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taiwan the previous year. A year later, the two leaders affirmed that humans, not AI, must control the decision to use nuclear weapons. And in late 2025, Beijing released a white paper emphatically reiterating its support for nuclear arms control and has moved toward more transparency by publishing more information, including in English, about its military upgrades.

Chinese leaders clearly do not want a war over Taiwan. Publicly, they repeatedly emphasize that their goal is “peaceful unification” and “winning without fighting,” invoking the Chinese strategist Sun-tzu. Beijing’s longtime “one country, two systems” policy toward Taiwan—which would bring the island under Chinese sovereignty while allowing it substantial autonomy—leaves room for a negotiated solution. Last year, in an important analysis of China’s strategic ambitions, the scholars David Kang, Jackie Wong, and Zenobia Chan examined 12,000 articles and hundreds of speeches by Xi to argue that Beijing prioritizes regime stability and internal development over displacing the United States as a global military hegemon. Although China’s major, unannounced exercises around Taiwan earlier this month may constitute an exception, overall, Chinese military exercises near Taiwan over the last five years are consistent with this interpretation: many have reacted to perceived provocations, illustrate only medium-scale capabilities, and have generally had a performative quality, accompanied by extensive press coverage.

There is still an opening for the United States and China to de-escalate. To achieve strategic stability, the two countries will need to make a concerted effort to defuse their security dilemma—the dynamic in which each side perceives the other’s defensive measures as aggressive. First, U.S. and Chinese leaders need to revive superpower summitry. Biden held only three face-to-face meetings with Xi on the sidelines of regional economic meetings. Although the May 2026 Beijing summit between Trump and Xi yielded no major breakthroughs, the meeting did improve the two leaders’ personal relationship; today, U.S.-Chinese tensions are lower than they were between 2021 and 2025. This progress suggests the great value of holding a regular, annual, multiday bilateral summit with a significant focus on nuclear arms control. Such meetings would give expert working groups time to methodically develop measures to reduce the risk of conflict. Just as important, the summits need to be long enough to leave room for unscripted conversations. At their first summit, in Geneva in November 1985, U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev famously broke away from anxious bureaucrats and advisers for an impromptu walk—an encounter that helped establish a more constructive relationship.

Industry observers note that the United States must also take concrete steps to reduce the chance of escalation in the Taiwan Strait. Above all, it should adhere more consistently to its “one China” policy—its position that Beijing is the sole legal government of China. More consistency would include limiting U.S. legislators’ trips to the island and downgrading U.S.-Taiwanese defense relations by, for example, holding meetings less frequently and at lower diplomatic levels. Washington should remind key allies such as Japan to proceed cautiously in terms of their rhetoric and military deployments. Such a restraint-oriented strategy would make it clear to Taiwan that independence is off the table, encouraging it to take a more accommodating approach that would lower the temperature with Beijing. If Washington were to agree to common-sense limitations on arms sales to Taiwan—such as refusing to sell Taiwan the surface-to-surface ballistic Army Tactical Missile System (ATACMS), which can reach across the strait to the Chinese mainland—Beijing would likely reciprocate by scaling back its military exercises and related military deployments around the island. There are real incentives for Beijing to de-escalate. Doing so could improve relations with neighbors such as Japan, free up focus for domestic priorities, lower military spending, and limit the chance of war.

Sources indicate that the Pentagon needs to demonstrate Washington’s intent to avoid war over Taiwan by gradually decreasing U.S. warship transits through the Taiwan Strait. Even more crucial, Washington should also substantially reduce U.S. military deployments in the Luzon Strait between Taiwan and the Philippines and around Japan’s Ryukyu Islands. Such deployments only exacerbate the security dilemma.

Exhibiting restraint does not mean the United States would be giving Taiwan away. The United States can continue to provide Taiwan with defensive arms (such as missile interceptors, artillery, drones, and mines) and harden U.S. bases in the region to provide stabilizing deterrence. But even if U.S. leaders publicly abjure direct military intervention to defend Taiwan—a rational step that would lower the risk of nuclear war—China will prefer negotiating with Taipei on the island’s autonomy over a bloody military showdown with Taiwanese forces. For their part, Taiwan’s leaders will likely accommodate themselves to limited self-governance under Chinese overall sovereignty. In the end, China’s main goal is to get Taiwan out of the U.S. sphere of influence. Chinese leaders’ major fear is not so much Taiwanese autonomy as the prospect of the island serving as a U.S. forward base—in Chinese parlance, “using Taiwan to contain China.”.

Another important step would be to seek a multilateral pledge by all nuclear-armed states to employ nuclear weapons only in retaliation against a nuclear attack. Such a policy would reduce the risk of miscalculation during a crisis. China has long embraced such a no-first-use policy, but U.S. leaders have traditionally opposed it, believing that it might expose U.S. allies to conventional attack. The U.S. nuclear deterrent for allies, however, increasingly lacks credibility because the costs of starting a nuclear war would vastly outweigh the benefits. And after the collapse of traditional nuclear arms control, a mutual no-first-use policy offers a promising area of common ground between the United States and China. It would reinforce the existing no-first-use policies of China and India and implicitly acknowledge their leadership in the area of nuclear restraint, a virtue when newer nuclear states are chafing under the old Cold War superpowers’ dominance of arms control. This approach could even entice Beijing into a wider, more comprehensive process of bilateral or multilateral nuclear arms control.

Beyond these three major initiatives, the United States and China should sign an agreement to notify each other about their ballistic missile tests. Washington could also consider giving Beijing a larger role in nonproliferation efforts, for instance by affording China leadership roles in negotiations and inspection regimes in future nonproliferation arrangements. The U.S. arms control agenda with China should focus not only on offensive nuclear systems but also on missile defenses and tactical nuclear weapons, as well as AI technologies. And it would help if the United States evolved its own nuclear posture in the direction of restraint by reducing its warheads, warfighting capabilities, and alert posture.

Ultimately, the United States needs to get serious about reining in an arms race with China before its perception that one is apace becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. The two countries have a mutual interest in restraint. If Washington continues to overlook Beijing’s incentives to compromise—and the real signs that it is willing to do so—an arms race that, as of now, is mostly putative will become a reality. And a catastrophic war that could have been avoided could indeed become inevitable.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Center for Security Policy President Tommy Waller warns that a string of outages affecting the NSA, banks and major technology systems raises national security concerns, even as officials rule out a coordinated cyberattack.

Recent findings suggest that U.S. adversaries have spent years developing ways to disrupt the country's critical infrastructure in a conflict, and the wave of technology disruptions affecting everything from banks to the National Security Agency has offered a reminder of how detrimental those failures could be even without a cyberattack.

The string of outages has fueled speculation about whether the incidents are connected, though Trump administration officials have ruled out a coordinated cyberattack.

National security experts caution that while the outages do not establish malicious activity, they underscore the stakes of protecting systems that underpin everything from financial transactions to military operations.

TIMELINE: AMERICA HITS A TECH WALL AS OUTAGES CRIPPLE EMAIL, GROUND FLIGHTS AND DISRUPT MAJOR BANKS.

"We know that our adversaries use that domain to attack our critical infrastructure," Tommy Waller, a national security expert with the Center for Security Policy, told Fox News Digital.

"Modern warfare, our people and our critical infrastructures are a prime target for all of our adversaries.".

It has been revealed that china accused the NSA of launching a cyberattack against its national time service. (Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty Images).

In a span of six days, technical disruptions affected Microsoft 365, commercial air travel, payroll and human resources software, banking transactions and the National Security Administration's highly classified internal communications network.

Some led to massive impacts on everyday life, including only the second-ever nationwide ground stop on all commercial flights since the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

"This is not a cyberattack, and this is not a coordinated effort by a nation-state," Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton remarked Tuesday on Fox Business' "The Claman Countdown.".

Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin similarly insisted the disruptions had "nothing to do with cyberattacks," suggesting that technical failures could become more common as new technology is introduced.

"I believe we're going to see more of this as newly introduced technology rolls out," Mullin stated Tuesday. A day earlier, he sought to reassure Americans during an appearance on Fox News' "Hannity," saying, "Well, breathe. The homeland is secure. Our banking system is secure.".

PRESIDENT TRUMP DOWNPLAYS PANIC OVER TECH OUTAGES: ‘NOBODY’S GOING TO PLAY GAMES WITH US’.

But the disruption at the NSA, one of the nation's most sophisticated intelligence agencies, has drawn particular scrutiny.

United Airlines planes parked at Newark Liberty International Airport in Newark, N.J., Nov. 3, 2025. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images).

Sources indicate that the agency's highly classified internal communications network, known as NSA Net, went down Tuesday, disrupting employees' ability to communicate classified information internally. Employee attendance at the agency's Fort Meade, Maryland, campus was "staggered" throughout the week to ease systems' use, and the network did not resume operations until Friday.

"This latest thing at the NSA is more problematic because their systems are generally not tied to anybody else, particularly their classified ones," national security and cybersecurity expert Steve Bucci told Fox News Digital.

"And, so, that being coincidentally, you know, in this sequence makes it a little harder to just write off.".

A U.S. official attributed the disruption to routine maintenance, saying the NSA experienced temporary interruptions to some internal systems but that its critical operations and national security capabilities remained fully functional.

Waller said the NSA outage could have been "self-induced" by efforts to patch vulnerabilities but questioned whether the broader string of disruptions was coincidental.

"The widespread and persistent nature of it and the types of infrastructures that are being targeted — appear to be targeted — that, to me, says that it's more than just a coincidence," he said.

Daniel Hoffman, a former CIA station chief and Fox News contributor, warned the institutions experiencing outages are already prime targets for foreign adversaries and cybercriminals.

Recent findings suggest that "Every single one of these entities is a target, and so are you and I," Hoffman told Fox News Digital. "Every single day, 24 hours a day, China, Russia, North Korea, Iran, criminals, hackers are trying to target the banks. They're trying to target Microsoft, obviously.".

Fox News Digital has reached out to the White House for comment.

In a recent development, the threat has already reached American infrastructure. In July, hackers targeted more than 30 municipal water systems in Minnesota, part of a broader wave of cyber intrusions across multiple states that forced some utilities to switch to manual operations and disrupted water service. Federal investigators examined possible Iranian involvement, though the attacks were not definitively attributed.

In a recent development, the Pentagon is also preparing for the possibility of widespread infrastructure failures during a major conflict. Under its FORTRESS initiative, military bases across the continental United States are being directed to prepare to sustain essential operations for at least 90 days without outside support, according to documents previously reviewed by Fox News Digital.

"We don't want to rely on standard civilian municipal infrastructure to run our national defense. We just simply can't. It's an intolerable risk," Pentagon chief spokesperson Sean Parnell previously told Fox News Digital.

Waller pointed to longstanding Chinese military writings that contemplate attacks on civilian communications and infrastructure during a conflict, arguing that the United States must consider the broader threat even when individual outages appear unrelated.

Industry observers note that "Again, I am not saying that China did this. But if China wanted to, this is in their doctrine, right?" Waller mentioned.

GROCERY STORE CYBERATTACKS ARE ‘PSYCHOLOGICAL WARFARE’ THAT COULD STRIKE US, FORMER FBI AGENT WARNS.

It has been revealed that in 2024, U.S. intelligence and law enforcement agencies warned that Chinese state-sponsored hackers known as Volt Typhoon had infiltrated American communications, energy, transportation and water systems, positioning themselves to potentially disrupt critical services during a conflict with the United States.

Latest research published last month found that the group had continued targeting government, defense and critical infrastructure networks through a separate hacking operation, even after U.S. authorities moved to dismantle parts of its infrastructure.

Bucci, however, noted that an adversary seeking to compromise American infrastructure might have little incentive to cause widespread, visible failures that could expose its activities.

Recent findings suggest that banking problems and widespread flight disruptions marked a stretch of technology troubles that also hit Microsoft and Workday. (Reuters).

"They might want to go in and do things to implant stuff for later use," Bucci stated when asked whether foreign adversaries could be testing vulnerabilities in critical U.S. infrastructure.

"But you usually don't do a weight test where you make stuff fail or get glitchy because that can then warn the target," he added.

The disruptions have also prompted calls for greater transparency from federal officials and private companies responsible for critical systems.

According to recent reports, "For our economy to function, people need to have some confidence in banks, among other things," Hoffman stated. "So, kind of need to tell us what's going on.".

Waller also urged greater transparency about infrastructure vulnerabilities and the steps being taken to address them.

Breaking: Sweeping permitting overhaul passes Senate, on to House

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1479 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mike Lee, R-Utah., Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., and Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., hold a news conference on the measure in the Capitol on Sept.
  • The Senate passed a bill Thursday evening that would overhaul the federal permitting system for electric power lines, power lines wind and solar farms, hard rock mining and oil drilling projects and more.
  • Recent findings suggest that it's the culmination of a yearslong effort intended to address industry concerns that it is too difficult to build any major infrastructure project in the United States.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From left, Sens. Mike Lee, R-Utah., Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., and Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., hold a news conference on the measure in the Capitol on Sept. 30. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

The Senate passed a bill Thursday evening that would overhaul the federal permitting system for electric power lines, power lines wind and solar farms, hard rock mining and oil drilling projects and more.

Recent findings suggest that it's the culmination of a yearslong effort intended to address industry concerns that it is too difficult to build any major infrastructure project in the United States. Supporters overcame opposition from more than half the Democratic Caucus, which will be a factor when the bill moves to the House after the Thanksgiving recess.

The bill passed on a 62-33 vote, with 31 Democrats joining two Republicans, Josh Hawley of Missouri and Mike Rounds of South Dakota, in opposition.

Shortly after the post-cloture time expired late Thursday, the Senate voted on passage of the legislation, including a substitute amendment consisting of revised text of the original permitting bill that the bipartisan authors unveiled before the midterm elections.

However, the chamber did not consider any additional amendments to the bill, as initially planned by the sponsors, including Environment and Public Works Chairman Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., panel ranking member Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., Energy and Natural Resources Chairman Mike Lee, R-Utah, and panel ranking member Martin Heinrich, D-N.M.

The bill includes changes to how reviews are conducted and permits are issued under the National Environmental Policy Act, National Historic Preservation Act, Endangered Species Act, Federal Power Act and Clean Water Act.

It includes provisions intended to ensure electricity ratepayers are not saddled with the costs of bringing power to data centers, and would give the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission newly introduced authority over interstate transmission lines.

It also would provide legal recourse when administrations discriminate against certain forms of energy or seek to revisit permits on ideological grounds. That's intended in part to address the Trump administration’s actions to delay or block solar and wind energy projects.

Democrats walked away from negotiations last year due to Trump administration actions to block offshore wind construction. However they ultimately stated they received sufficient assurances that the administration would let stalled wind and solar projects move forward.

The "big four" senators on the permitting bill solicited feedback and changes sought by various lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, and were open to votes on additional amendments — so long as they didn't undo the measure's core tenets.

"This bill has threaded a needle the likes of which this chamber has not seen in a while, and we’ve got to take advantage of this opportunity," Capito said before passage.

In a recent development, ultimately, Oregon Democratic Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden would not consent to a time agreement allowing consideration of a finite number of amendments because Republicans wouldn't allow up-or-down votes at a simple-majority threshold on some of theirs. Merkley then objected to a unanimous consent request to consider amendments on the floor.

Wyden was pushing for a vote on an amendment that would prohibit construction of data centers on federal public lands. Merkley was pushing for amendments that included barring data centers from benefiting from “project certainty” protections against future presidents revoking their permits, and limiting presidential power to impose tariffs on clean energy project components, like wind turbines.

In a recent development, the Senate had already adopted the substitute amendment introduced by the bill’s sponsors during a procedural vote on Wednesday. But the lack of a unanimous consent agreement to take up more amendments meant that an additional manager's package of changes to the substitute fell by the wayside.

That amendment would have narrowed the instances where exemptions from National Historic Preservation Act reviews would be allowed, increased the annual authorization for the Historic Preservation Fund by 50 percent, and addressed concerns about the use of eminent domain when permitting transmission projects raised by Hawley and Rounds.

The sponsors introduced an updated version of their manager’s amendment Thursday afternoon that would refine exemptions from the ratepayer projection provisions so that artificial intelligence "hyperscalers" can't escape through a loophole.

The original manager's amendment sought to exempt internet and telecommunications providers' facilities, but the language was broad enough that cloud storage and other "information services" exclusions could potentially benefit data centers.

None of those changes made it into the bill as a result of the stalemate over amendments, and Merkley objected on the floor to incorporating just the manager's package.

The bill has been endorsed by a wide range of industry groups, who argue that the current federal permitting regime makes it too difficult to finance, strategy and construct projects domestically. This includes the American Petroleum Institute, the American Clean Power Association, the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the National Association of Manufacturers.

The White House expressed its support for the bill in a statement of administration policy this month.

The bill now moves on to the House, where it seemingly has the votes to pass.

Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., mentioned last week that the bill can pass in that chamber, while a number of Democrats including the centrist Blue Dog Coalition and Reps. Scott Peters, D-Calif., co-chair of the bipartisan Climate Solutions Caucus, and Nikki Budzinski, D-Ill., have expressed support.

Budzinski was elected chair of the 112-member Newly introduced Democrat Coalition last week for the next Congress, and that group issued a statement speaking favorably of permitting while stopping short of endorsing the bill as right now drafted.

However, attendance on the House GOP side after Thanksgiving could be an concern: more than 30 lawmakers regularly skipped votes this week, the majority of them Republicans.

And many Democrats have called on Heinrich and Whitehouse to punt consideration of the bill to the upcoming Congress, when their party will have large majorities in both chambers.

According to recent reports, merkley, who is in line to chair the Environment and Public Works Committee, and House Natural Resources ranking member Jared Huffman, D-Calif. — the expected chairman of that panel — both said the bill included too many provisions Democrats opposed in order to garner Republican support.

Industry observers note that some of the nation’s largest environmental groups including the Sierra Club and Natural Resources Defense Council oppose the bill. A coalition of 17 Democratic states also expressed their opposition. And some Native American tribes and organizations, including the National Congress of American Indians, also expressed their opposition.

"I’m hoping to have a full opportunity to address the many legitimate concerns that stakeholders have raised with this bill," Merkley said before the vote Thursday night.

But Heinrich and Whitehouse resisted calls to delay the bill, arguing that President Donald Trump is in office for two more years and that any bill needs his support to be signed into law. They added that they will be able to address environmental complications under their majority, and that this bill would represent the “floor” of their ambitions.

While Republicans have called for changes to the federal permitting system for decades, the effort gained steam with Democrats after the passage of their 2022 reconciliation law, which they dubbed the Inflation Reduction Act, or IRA.

Sources indicate that as part of the deal to get then-Senate Energy and Natural Resources Chairman Joe Manchin III, D-W.Va., on board with the IRA, the Biden administration agreed to support a bill overhauling the federal permitting system. Manchin introduced a bill that included changes to NEPA and transmission permitting, and would approve all remaining permits needed for the Mountain Valley Pipeline in his home state.

However, his effort ultimately fell short on a 47-47 procedural vote to attach the bill to that year’s defense authorization measure.

In the 118th Congress Manchin tried again, and in 2024 he and then-Energy and Natural Resources ranking member John Barrasso, R-Wyo., introduced what Manchin called a “perfectly crafted balance.” The committee approved that bill in July 2024, but it was never voted on by the full Senate.

Capito, Whitehouse, Lee and Heinrich made a collective commitment to address permitting overhaul when they stepped into their current roles in January 2025, and spent nearly 21 months working on the legislation.

Since Manchin’s first bill, the political calculus changed.

After decades of stagnant energy demand, electricity prices began rising in part due to the expansion of data centers. Consumers also became increasingly frustrated with their local utilities over affordability concerns, which in turn spurred more lawmakers across the country, including on Capitol Hill, to critically examine their practices.

According to recent reports, lee also pushed for language streamlining NHPA reviews, which had not been a focus of earlier permitting discussion. He's argued that the law has expanded beyond its originally intended scope and become a major barrier to infrastructure projects in Western states like Utah.
